The story behind an idea

The wandering womb: the long history of "hysteria"

For centuries the womb was blamed for unexplained symptoms. Today we speak of functional neurological disorders, which men have too.

Some texts of Greek medicine described the womb as an organ that could wander through the body and cause breathlessness, fainting or paralysis. From the Greek word hystera, womb, comes hysteria, a diagnosis applied for centuries mainly to women.

Charcot and Freud

In the 19th century, the neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot studied patients at the Salpêtrière in Paris who had seizures and paralysis without visible damage, and argued that men could have them too. Sigmund Freud attended his lectures and developed the idea that such symptoms had a psychological origin.

The word "hysteria" disappeared from the manuals in 1980. Today we speak of functional neurological disorder: real symptoms, such as weakness, tremor or seizures, caused by a problem in how the nervous system functions rather than by damage. It is common in neurology clinics and is treatable, especially with specialised physiotherapy and psychotherapy.

References

  1. Tasca, C. et al. (2012). Women and hysteria in the history of mental health. Clinical Practice and Epidemiology in Mental Health, 8, 110–119.
  2. Stone, J. (2016). Functional neurological disorders: the neurological assessment as treatment. Practical Neurology, 16(1), 7–17.
